Essentials 2.0 · Flow inspiration · 08-debrief-review

Debrief and review: ideas from other products

This page shows examples from other products for the Debrief and review module of Essentials 2.0, grouped by product. They cover rewatching recorded simulation sessions and a QR code that turns a faculty member's phone into a second screen. They also cover AI debrief summaries and clips, recording the debrief itself, group grading, and downloading or sharing recordings. Access to recordings from a course, live control during recording, and the general mobile app are covered by other modules. Sources: the design reference libraries Mobbin and Refero, researched on 30 September 2026.

What we have today. The session video review screen (SRV) from LearningSpace is reused. Video sits on the left. Right-panel tabs are Annotation, Data Entry, Layout and Transcript. A timeline split into chapters has clickable manual and AI annotation markers, plus a searchable transcript labelled by speaker. Today faculty annotations are visible to learners on the debrief-room screen, which faculty dislike. The concept: when the recording ends, the SRV shows a QR for the debrief. Faculty scan it and get a phone web page with their annotations, AI annotations, the AI summary and AI clips. The big screen shows only the video, controlled from the phone. The debrief audio is captured and turned into AI notes, with a phone voice memo as fallback.

How to read this page

Each section below is one product. Each strip of screenshots is one flow: a real sequence of screens, in the order a user sees them. Click a screenshot to enlarge it. "Worth borrowing" lists ideas we could use, and "Avoid" lists what we should not copy. Use the task filters to see only one task, and click ☆ on a flow to add it to your own shortlist.

12 products · 19 flows · 87 screens · 8 tasks

What the best products have in common

  1. AI claims link to the moment that proves them Grain, Fireflies and Otter all attach times to AI summary items (outcomes, action items, outline entries), and a click jumps both video and transcript. This is how 'evidence-linked moments' work in an AI debrief, and it maps onto the SRV's clickable AI annotation markers. None of the three puts an approval step between the AI text and the Share button.See: Grain: Meeting detail · Fireflies: Generating summary details · Otter AI: Conversation detail
  2. Human checks come before the AI runs or at publishing, not after the summary The review steps found are at the edges. Fireflies makes you preview a custom AI prompt on at least two past meetings before it runs. Descript asks for clip count, duration and topic before Submit. Fireflies soundbites need a title and an access level before Done. AI summaries themselves (Grain, Otter web) go straight to Share. Essentials needs both: faculty criteria up front and an explicit reveal before learners or the big screen see AI output.See: Fireflies: Preview notes · Descript: Creating clips · Fireflies: Creating a soundbite · Otter AI: Conversation detail
  3. The big screen shows join controls briefly; control lives on the phone Canva's presenting screen shows a QR, a short code for phones that will not scan, a live participant count and a Hide control. Hide clears the banner once people have joined. Its phone flow and Google TV's put playback controls, seeking and connection status on the phone only, so the shared display stays clean. No single flow shows both sides at once. Canva's two flows together come closest.See: Canva: Starting a session · Canva: Share remote control · Google TV: Remote (movie)
  4. Share policy is set beside the video, with expiry presets and a separate download switch Frame.io keeps share settings in a sidebar next to playback with relative expiry presets. Dropbox splits view from edit links and confirms 'Restrictions apply' after saving. Fireflies asks who can access a clip at the moment it is created. All three treat download as its own switch, separate from viewing. None shows a consent or confirmation step before the download itself.See: Frame.io: Scheduling an expiration date · Dropbox: Editing share settings · Fireflies: Creating a soundbite
  5. Group-first feedback and individual rubrics are separate products today ClassDojo awards one skill to a whole group in a single tap, confirms it with a large message and Undo, and reports whole-class first with a path into each learner. Grain scores one speaker at a time against a rubric under the video and sends the result to that person. The usual case in Essentials needs ClassDojo's group default with Grain's rubric and per-person override in the same screen. No product shows the combination.See: ClassDojo: Adding a point to a group · ClassDojo: Reports detail · Grain: Scoring a speaker
  6. Phone capture keeps recording in the background and accepts markers while live Otter shows a live transcript with one-tap highlight, comment and photo markers during recording. Beside offers a dedicated in-person mode and a floating recorder that keeps working while you move around the app. Both end in an overview (summary, transcript, to-dos) attached to the conversation record. This is the pattern for capturing the debrief discussion on the faculty phone. Neither asks participants for consent.See: Otter AI: Recording a conversation (extended) · Beside: Recording in-person meetings
  7. Speaker-aware transcripts double as a participation view Grain colours transcript speakers to match a talk-time timeline under the video. Otter shows talk-time percentages and lets you rematch speakers who were labelled wrong. In a team simulation this is formative data (who led, who stayed silent), and speaker correction matters because AI labelling in a noisy sim room will be wrong.See: Grain: Watching a video · Grain: Meeting detail · Otter AI: Conversation detail

Questions we still need to answer

  • Camera views are a clear gap. No Mobbin or Refero flow shows switching between camera angles or controlling a remote-controlled camera that pans, tilts and zooms (PTZ) during playback of a recording. DAZN and Tesla were fetched for this but show a highlights shelf and a clip library. Google Maps is the only 360 evidence and it is free outdoor roaming, not a fixed room on a timeline. Multi-camera sim review needs its own prototype or research outside these sources.
  • No source shows the full second-screen handoff in one flow, and none shows private notes on the phone while the shared screen stays clean. Canva and Google TV only show remote control. All phone-side evidence is phone-sized, so the tablet-versus-phone conflict is not settled by this research.
  • What should 'faculty approve' mean with a group waiting in the debrief room? Every AI summary observed shares immediately. The checks found are at setup or clip level. Nobody has tested whether to reveal items one at a time on the big screen, or keep everything hidden until faculty release it.
  • Consent is missing everywhere. Beside and Otter start recording an in-person conversation without a consent prompt. Dropbox and Frame.io can disable downloads but show no confirm-before-download step. Both the recording-faculty-speech consent and the download consent need original design.
  • ClassDojo's group feedback is behaviour points for school children and Grain's scorecard grades one person. How a group rubric with per-person overrides is stored, reported and released to each learner is open.
  • No example shows how long AI clips take to make. Descript and Fireflies generate clips from recordings that already exist, and no screen shows how long generation takes. The 'clips ready immediately after the session' constraint needs a technical answer, not a gallery one.

Grain

Close match3 flows

Grain is the closest twin of the SRV. AI outcomes and action items carry times that jump the video. Transcript search stays in sync with a speaker talk-time timeline. A rubric scorecard sits under the video and is sent to one named learner. The AI summary is live with Share before anyone approves it.

WebMobbin4 steps

Meeting detail

From the meetings list, the user opens a recording and reviews the AI summary, then the chapters. Time-linked bullets sit next to the video, above a timeline of who spoke when.

AI-based debriefing (formative and summative)Rewatch videos

Worth borrowing

  • A first-time tip, 'Skip to the important parts', teaches that the times on AI outcomes jump the video and transcript to that moment (screen 2).
  • Outcomes and action items each carry clickable times that link a claim to the moment that supports it (screens 2 to 3).
  • A speaker timeline under the video shows each person's share of talk time as coloured bars, with empty Comments and Clips rows ready for markers (screen 3).
  • The chapter list nests time-linked bullets under each chapter, and the chapter name appears on the video's progress bar (screen 4).

Avoid

  • The AI summary and chapters go live with Share and Ask AI straight away, with no step for faculty to edit or approve before learners see them. The baseline wants human review.

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: adds AI chapters, outcomes and action items to the SRV's Annotation and Transcript tabs. It clashes with the baseline if AI notes appear on the debrief big screen automatically.

WebMobbin3 steps

Watching a video

The user opens a meeting review, switches from Summary to a searchable speaker-labelled Transcript synced to video, then uses a focused player with 10s skips and 1x speed.

Rewatch videos

Worth borrowing

  • Transcript search highlights each match ('Grain'), and speaker colours match the bars on the timeline (screen 2).
  • The Transcript tab sits next to Summary and Chapters in the same panel, so one click checks an AI claim against what was said (screen 2).
  • A stripped-down player keeps only the chapter name, 10-second skips and a visible 1x speed, so nothing competes with the video on the room display (screen 3).

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: matches the SRV layout of video on the left and Transcript and Annotation tabs on the right. The stripped-down player could be the big-screen mode while the phone holds the notes.

WebMobbin8 steps

Scoring a speaker

In a coaching review, the user picks a scorecard for one speaker and answers yes/no and 1 to 5 items with notes. After submitting, the results appear under the video with 'Send to Sam'.

Group grading

Worth borrowing

  • Rubric rows with coloured 1 to 5 buttons and a large average score sit beside the video of all participants, so faculty grade while rewatching (screen 1).
  • A new scorecard asks for the speaker, the scorecard template and who can view it before scoring starts (screen 3).
  • 'Submit' stays disabled until required answers are filled in, and each item offers N/A (screens 4 to 5).
  • A 'Send to Sam' button stays in view and sends the finished review to one named learner (screens 1 and 8).

Avoid

  • It scores one speaker at a time, with no way to grade the whole team and adjust individuals in one pass. That misses group grading, which the baseline says is the usual case.

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: adds a rubric under the video and sharing with a named learner to the SRV's Data Entry tab. It is useful for adjusting one person's grade, but the default needs to start from the group.

Fireflies

Same task, different field3 flows

Fireflies is the only product that previews AI output on past meetings before the AI runs for real. It also has the clearest human-finished clip: you drag across the highlighted transcript to select a clip, then add a title and choose 'Who can access' before Done.

WebMobbin4 steps

Preview notes

In step 1 of 2 of creating an AI app, the author writes an AI prompt, picks at least two meetings, and turns on 'Preview Notes' before moving on.

AI-based debriefing (formative and summative)

Worth borrowing

  • The screen puts the plain-language instructions on the left and 'select meetings to preview / refine from output' on the right (screen 1).
  • 'Preview Notes' stays disabled until at least two meetings are chosen, which forces a trial run (screens 1 to 4).
  • 'Preview Notes' comes before 'Next', so a person checks the output before finishing setup (screen 4).

Avoid

  • The flow never shows step 2 or a share or publish screen, so it is weak evidence for approving before learners see anything. It only covers previewing during setup.

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: faculty could set what the AI should pull out of sim recordings and preview it on past sessions before it runs on live debriefs.

View on Mobbin ↗
WebMobbin3 steps

Generating summary details

The user opens a meeting, reads the general summary and notes with time links, searches the speaker-labelled transcript or asks AskFred, and controls playback (speed, 10-second skips, download, Share).

AI-based debriefing (formative and summative)Rewatch videos

Worth borrowing

  • AI notes contain blue time links (for example 06:33) that jump from a claim to that moment in the recording (screen 1).
  • AskFred, a tab next to Transcript, keeps questions about the recording beside the searchable transcript (screens 1 to 3).
  • One bar at the bottom holds 1x speed, 10-second skips, Download and thumbs up or down on the AI output (screen 1).

Avoid

  • Share is available as soon as the AI summary appears, with no edit or approve step before sharing. That goes against the human review in the baseline.

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: the closest Fireflies match to the SRV's summary, transcript and playback. Use it for AI debrief text linked to evidence, but add a faculty approval before learners can see it.

WebMobbin5 steps

Creating a soundbite

From the clips panel, the user drags across a range to make a soundbite while the transcript highlights it. They then name the clip, pick a playlist and who can access it, and tap Done.

AI-provided short clipsDownload videos and share recordings easily

Worth borrowing

  • 'Create Soundbite' (by hand) and 'AI Soundbite' sit side by side (screen 1).
  • Dragging across the recording, with START and END fields, colours the chosen part of the transcript purple so it can be checked before creating (screens 2 to 3).
  • Tabs for 'Magic Soundbite' and 'Keyword Soundbite' offer other ways to make clips without leaving the window (screen 2).
  • After creating, the window asks for a title and 'Who can access' (Participants only) before Done, so a person finishes the clip (screen 4).

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: a strong model for human review of AI clips before publishing. Trim against the transcript, publish with permissions, and attach the clip once faculty tap Done.

Canva

Same task, different field2 flows

Canva is the only flow that shows the big-screen side of a QR handoff. It shows a large QR plus short code, a live participant count, and a Hide control that clears the join banner from the public display. The phone side hands out remote control by QR or link, with Pause.

WebMobbin3 steps

Starting a session

The presenter starts a live session on the big screen, where a QR code and a short code let the audience join. The join banner can then be hidden while the session stays live.

Separate app or QR: see notes and annotations

Worth borrowing

  • People can join through a large QR code, the canva.live address or a short code, which helps in rooms where phones struggle to scan (screen 2).
  • A live count of participants next to 'End session' shows the presenter that people have joined (screen 2).
  • Hide and Show on the join strip clear the join details from the public display once people are connected (screens 2 to 3).
  • 'Copy invitation' gives people who join remotely or late a way in without the QR code (screen 2).

Avoid

  • This flow shows only the big-screen side, with no phone notes or remote screens, so it is weak evidence for private faculty annotations.

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: a strong pattern for the QR code on the debrief-room screen after recording. The public display shows the video and join details for a short time; the phone would hold the private annotations.

iOSMobbin2 steps

Share remote control

From a presentation on the phone, the user opens remote control with a QR code and a link to copy, to hand control to another device, with a pause option.

Separate app or QR: see notes and annotations

Worth borrowing

  • The title 'Remote control this presentation' says what the screen is for in one line (screen 2).
  • An 'Available' status and a Pause control let the presenter switch off the remote link without ending the session (screen 2).
  • A 'Copy link' next to the QR code covers phones or tablets that fail to scan in a debrief room (screen 2).

Avoid

  • The flow shows only the phone, never the big screen it controls, so Essentials still needs both sides designed before this counts as strong second-screen evidence.

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: maps to the faculty phone as a private remote for the room display. Pair it with the web Live QR flow so both sides are designed.

Google TV

Same task, different field1 flow

Google TV uses the phone as the full playback remote. 'Watch on TV' hands playback to the big screen, and a persistent 'Living Room TV' bar confirms the connection. The progress bar and 30-second skip buttons appear only on the phone.

iOSMobbin2 steps

Remote (movie)

From a movie page on the phone, the user taps 'Watch on TV' while connected to the living-room TV. The phone then works as a remote with a touch pad, volume and a progress bar.

Separate app or QR: see notes and annotations

Worth borrowing

  • A bar at the bottom shows the title and a green 'Living Room TV' connection while you browse, so control stays one tap away (screen 1).
  • 'Watch on TV' is the main button, which makes handing playback from the phone to the big screen explicit (screen 1).
  • A dedicated remote screen shows 'Connected' at the top, a swipe pad, 30-second skips and a progress bar for precise jumps (screen 2).
  • Playback controls are only on the phone, so the TV shows only the video, which matches the privacy goal (screen 2).

Avoid

  • An installed-app remote with arrow pad and Assistant buttons is heavier than needed. The baseline prefers a simple web page on a phone or tablet for faculty who are not technical.

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: the closest pattern from another field for a second screen. The phone controls playback, and the big screen appears to show video only. It is weak on annotations but strong on showing the connection.

Otter AI

Same task, different field2 flows

Otter AI captures a conversation on the phone with a live transcript and one-tap highlight, comment and photo markers while recording. Its web review is this module's example of what not to do: the AI summary can be copied, shared or posted to Slack with no edit or approve step.

iOSMobbin11 steps

Recording a conversation (extended)

The user starts from Home, records with a live transcript and markers, browses Summary, Chat and Comments, then returns to Home with an AI summary snippet and image.

Record the debriefing and attach the evaluation to reportsAI-based debriefing (formative and summative)

Worth borrowing

  • The recording bar offers one-tap highlight, comment and image while live (screens 6 to 7).
  • An empty Chat states 'Chat is visible to all conversation participants' so visibility is clear up front (screen 4).
  • The Summary tab shows 'Creating a live summary...' placeholders during capture (screen 3).
  • The Home card shows an AI bullet and attached visual before opening the note (screen 10).

Avoid

  • AI summary and Share appear with no faculty approve or edit check before others can see them, which clashes with human-review-before-share for AI debrief.

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: matches using the phone to capture the debrief and as a second screen for private notes. It needs an approval step before learners see a summary.

Conversation detail

Descript

Same task, different field1 flow

Descript has a person set the rules for AI clips first: clip count, duration, layout and an optional topic before Submit. You can still change where each clip starts and ends by editing the transcript text.

WebMobbin5 steps

Creating clips

In an editor where the transcript and video stay in step, the user opens Underlord's 'Repurpose' tools. They set up 'Create clips' (number, length, layout, optional topic) and reach caption styles before Submit.

AI-provided short clipsRewatch videos

Worth borrowing

  • 'Create clips' asks for the number of clips, their length, a layout and an optional topic before Submit (screens 3 to 5).
  • The Repurpose menu also offers 'Create highlight reel' and 'Find highlights' next to 'Create clips' (screen 1).
  • The transcript is lined up word by word with the timeline, so the start and end of each clip can still be changed by editing text (screens 1 to 5).
  • A person sets the rules and then taps Submit, so clips are never published silently (screens 3 to 5).

Avoid

  • 'Viral bait' and social-media layouts are the wrong tone for clinical debrief highlights; use clinical topics to choose clips instead.

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: the best reference for AI clips where a person sets the rules before sharing. Bring the topic, number and length settings into the SRV phone review, and drop the social layouts.

Frame.io

Close match1 flow

Frame.io keeps share settings in a sidebar next to the video: expiry presets (24 hours, 1 week, 2 weeks) above a calendar, a passphrase, and a separate Downloads switch.

WebMobbin4 steps

Scheduling an expiration date

From the share sidebar, the user sets an expiration via presets or calendar, confirms Dec 31 11:59pm, and lands on a set expiry with Edit or clear.

Download videos and share recordings easily

Worth borrowing

  • Share settings stay in a side panel next to the video, so the user sets them without leaving the review (screen 1).
  • Quick choices ('24 Hours', '1 Week', '2 Weeks') sit above a calendar and time picker, which suits short sharing windows after a debrief (screen 2).
  • The chosen expiry ('Dec 31 at 11:59pm') is then shown in one short line with Edit and an X to clear it (screens 3 to 4).
  • Comments, Downloads and 'Show all versions' are separate switches next to Security (passphrase and expiry) (screens 1 and 4).

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: the best match for sharing video after a debrief, with settings next to playback, quick expiry choices and a Downloads switch. Essentials still needs consent before identifiable learners can be downloaded.

Dropbox

Same task, different field1 flow

Dropbox has the most detailed link settings: separate view and edit links, expiry, password and a switch to block downloads. It warns clearly about who the link reaches, and shows 'Restrictions apply' under 'Copy link' after saving.

WebMobbin9 steps

Editing share settings

The user opens Share, opens link settings, turns on expiration, password and disable-downloads, saves, and returns to the share sheet with restrictions acknowledged.

Download videos and share recordings easily

Worth borrowing

  • Separate tabs for 'Link for editing' and 'Link for viewing' keep viewing and download rules apart from editing rights (screens 1 to 2).
  • Switches for Expiration, Require password and Disable downloads stay off until needed (screens 2 to 8).
  • A yellow note, 'This applies only within Dropbox', appears when downloads are disabled, which is honest about the limit (screen 8).
  • After saving, the share window shows 'Restrictions apply · Modify' under 'Copy link' and a 'Settings saved' message (screen 9).

Avoid

  • Nine nearly identical screens for one setting task are too long; Essentials should keep expiry, password and download on one small panel.

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: adds a password, a download block and a clear 'restrictions apply' note to expiring share links for learners. Sim video of identifiable learners still needs consent before download.

ClassDojo

Outside idea2 flows

ClassDojo gives feedback to the group first. Faculty award a rubric-like skill to a whole group in one tap, with a big confirmation and 'Undo'. A whole-class report then opens into each learner's dated log.

WebMobbin3 steps

Adding a point to a group

The teacher opens Group A, awards a shared skill point to the whole group, and sees an on-screen confirmation with the group total updated.

Group grading

Worth borrowing

  • The group's members are listed first, then one main 'Award group' button, before any grade is given (screen 1).
  • A fixed set of skill buttons (+1 Helping others, On task, Participating, Persistence, Teamwork, Working hard) applies to the whole group at once (screen 2).
  • A large, brief confirmation ('Group A · +1 for Persistence') and 'Undo last' let the teacher fix a wrong tap straight away (screen 3).

Avoid

  • The side panel highlights one member (Sam) while the title says 'Give feedback to Group A', so it is unclear whether the award goes to the group or one person. Essentials needs an explicit choice between group grade and individual adjustment.

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: supports grading the group first. Skill buttons map to rubric items for the sim team, with 'Undo last' before the evaluation is locked.

WebMobbin4 steps

Reports detail

The teacher opens Options then View reports, inspects Whole-class points with a per-student sidebar and activity log, then switches to the Whole-class attendance week view.

Group grading

Worth borrowing

  • The report's side list shows 'Whole class' first, then each learner with a percentage, so one click goes from the group to one person (screen 3).
  • Points earned, skills awarded, Export and Print, and an all-time range sit in the same header (screen 3).

Beside

Same task, different field1 flow

Beside has a dedicated in-person recorder with a floating control that keeps recording while you navigate. It ends in an overview with the transcript and AI to-dos, which is the model for the phone voice-memo fallback. No consent prompt is shown.

iOSMobbin5 steps

Recording in-person meetings

The user turns on In-Person Recorder in Settings, starts a floating background recording with a live waveform, then lands on a Meeting Overview with transcript, share targets and short playback.

Record the debriefing and attach the evaluation to reportsAI-based debriefing (formative and summative)Download videos and share recordings easily

Worth borrowing

  • Settings has its own 'In-Person Recorder' switch, so recording a conversation in the room is a clear mode, not a one-off (screens 1 to 2).
  • A floating recorder with a timer, sound wave and stop button stays on screen while the user moves around the app (screens 3 to 4).
  • After the session, an overview shows a transcript link, sharing to Slack, email or notes, and playback with 'See Transcription' (screen 5).
  • When the AI finds nothing to do, the to-do list says 'No actions, you're in the clear!' (screen 5).

Google Maps

Outside idea1 flow

Google Maps is the only 360 look-around evidence found. An immersive view splits with a 2D map whose peg shows where you are facing. You can switch capture dates without leaving 360.

iOSMobbin6 steps

360 view

From a place page, the user enters the 360° street view and moves with arrows on the ground. A split screen adds a map whose marker shows which way they face, and older dates and recent photos are one tap away.

360 camera and PTZ in review

Worth borrowing

  • The 360° view splits with a flat map whose marker points the way you face (screens 4 to 5). That could become a room layout next to 360° playback.
  • Arrows on the ground move between capture points without leaving the 360° view (screens 2 to 3).
  • 'See more dates' and 'Latest photos' switch to another capture date or to still photos of the same place without leaving 360° (screens 3 and 6).
  • There are two ways in: a Street View marker on the map and an Immersive View card among the photos (screen 1).

Avoid

  • Roaming freely through outdoor panoramas is not the same as moving through a fixed 360° recording of a sim room; do not make endless walking the main debrief control.

What it means for Essentials Debrief and review: a fallback for camera views, since Tesla showed no multi-camera switching. A map that shows your direction next to the 360° view is the idea to borrow for 360° review beside SRV playback.
